title: Atomic structure: nucleus and electron shells
statement: understand that atoms are mostly empty space surrounding a very small, dense nucleus that contains protons and neutrons; electrons are found in shells in the empty space around the nucleus

title: Charges and masses of subatomic particles
statement: identify and describe protons, neutrons and electrons in terms of their relative charges and relative masses

title: Atomic, proton, mass and nucleon number
statement: understand the terms atomic and proton number; mass and nucleon number

title: Distribution of mass and charge in an atom
statement: describe the distribution of mass and charge within an atom

title: Deflection of particle beams in an electric field
statement: describe the behaviour of beams of protons, neutrons and electrons moving at the same velocity in an electric field

title: Counting protons, neutrons and electrons
statement: determine the numbers of protons, neutrons and electrons present in both atoms and ions given atomic or proton number, mass or nucleon number and charge

title: Trends in atomic and ionic radius
statement: state and explain qualitatively the variations in atomic radius and ionic radius across a period and down a group

title: Definition of isotope
statement: define the term isotope in terms of numbers of protons and neutrons

title: Isotope nuclide notation
statement: understand the notation $^{x}_{y}\mathrm{A}$ for isotopes, where $x$ is the mass or nucleon number and $y$ is the atomic or proton number

title: Isotopes and chemical properties
statement: state that and explain why isotopes of the same element have the same chemical properties

title: Isotopes and physical properties
statement: state that and explain why isotopes of the same element have different physical properties, limited to mass and density

title: Shells, sub-shells, orbitals and quantum number
statement: understand the terms: (a) shells, sub-shells and orbitals (b) principal quantum number ($n$) (c) ground state, limited to electronic configuration

title: Orbitals and electron capacity of s, p, d
statement: describe the number of orbitals making up s, p and d sub-shells, and the number of electrons that can fill s, p and d sub-shells

title: Energy order of sub-shells
statement: describe the order of increasing energy of the sub-shells within the first three shells and the 4s and 4p sub-shells

title: Writing electronic configurations
statement: describe the electronic configurations to include the number of electrons in each shell, sub-shell and orbital

title: Electron configuration and inter-electron repulsion
statement: explain the electronic configurations in terms of energy of the electrons and inter-electron repulsion

title: Deducing electronic configuration of atoms and ions
statement: determine the electronic configuration of atoms and ions given the atomic or proton number and charge, using either of the following conventions: e.g. for Fe: $1s^2 2s^2 2p^6 3s^2 3p^6 3d^6 4s^2$ (full electronic configuration) or $\ce{[Ar]}\,3d^6 4s^2$ (shorthand electronic configuration)

title: Electrons-in-boxes notation
statement: understand and use the electrons in boxes notation, e.g. for Fe: $\ce{[Ar]}$ 3d and 4s sub-shells shown as boxes with arrows representing paired and unpaired electrons

title: Shapes of s and p orbitals
statement: describe and sketch the shapes of s and p orbitals

title: Definition of a free radical
statement: describe a free radical as a species with one or more unpaired electrons

title: Definition of first ionisation energy
statement: define and use the term first ionisation energy, $IE_1$

title: Equations for successive ionisation energies
statement: construct equations to represent first, second and subsequent ionisation energies

title: Trends in ionisation energy across period and group
statement: identify and explain the trends in ionisation energies across a period and down a group of the Periodic Table

title: Successive ionisation energies of an element
statement: identify and explain the variation in successive ionisation energies of an element

title: Ionisation energy and nuclear attraction
statement: understand that ionisation energies are due to the attraction between the nucleus and the outer electron

title: Factors affecting ionisation energy
statement: explain the factors influencing the ionisation energies of elements in terms of nuclear charge, atomic/ionic radius, shielding by inner shells and sub-shells and spin-pair repulsion

title: Deducing electron configuration from ionisation data
statement: deduce the electronic configurations of elements using successive ionisation energy data

title: Deducing periodic table position from ionisation data
statement: deduce the position of an element in the Periodic Table using successive ionisation energy data

title: Definition of the unified atomic mass unit
statement: define the unified atomic mass unit as one twelfth of the mass of a carbon-12 atom

title: Relative atomic, isotopic, molecular and formula mass
statement: define relative atomic mass, $A_r$, relative isotopic mass, relative molecular mass, $M_r$, and relative formula mass in terms of the unified atomic mass unit

title: The mole and the Avogadro constant
statement: define and use the term mole in terms of the Avogadro constant

title: Writing formulas of ionic compounds
statement: write formulas of ionic compounds from ionic charges and oxidation numbers (shown by a Roman numeral), including: (a) the prediction of ionic charge from the position of an element in the Periodic Table (b) recall of the names and formulas for the following ions: $\ce{NO3-}$, $\ce{CO3^2-}$, $\ce{SO4^2-}$, $\ce{OH-}$, $\ce{NH4+}$, $\ce{Zn^2+}$, $\ce{Ag+}$, $\ce{HCO3-}$, $\ce{PO4^3-}$

title: Writing and balancing chemical equations
statement: (a) write and construct equations (which should be balanced), including ionic equations (which should not include spectator ions) (b) use appropriate state symbols in equations

title: Empirical and molecular formula definitions
statement: define and use the terms empirical and molecular formula

title: Anhydrous, hydrated and water of crystallisation
statement: understand and use the terms anhydrous, hydrated and water of crystallisation

title: Calculating empirical and molecular formulas
statement: calculate empirical and molecular formulas, using given data

title: Mole calculations: masses, volumes, concentrations, yield
statement: perform calculations including use of the mole concept, involving: (a) reacting masses (from formulas and equations) including percentage yield calculations (b) volumes of gases (e.g. in the burning of hydrocarbons) (c) volumes and concentrations of solutions (d) limiting reagent and excess reagent (e) deduce stoichiometric relationships from calculations such as those in 2.4.1(a)-(d)

title: Definition of electronegativity
statement: define electronegativity as the power of an atom to attract electrons to itself

title: Factors affecting electronegativity
statement: explain the factors influencing the electronegativities of the elements in terms of nuclear charge, atomic radius and shielding by inner shells and sub-shells

title: Trends in electronegativity
statement: state and explain the trends in electronegativity across a period and down a group of the Periodic Table

title: Predicting bond type from electronegativity difference
statement: use the differences in Pauling electronegativity values to predict the formation of ionic and covalent bonds (the presence of covalent character in some ionic compounds will not be assessed) (Pauling electronegativity values will be given where necessary)

title: Definition of ionic bonding
statement: define ionic bonding as the electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions (positively charged cations and negatively charged anions)

title: Describing ionic bonding in NaCl, MgO, CaF2
statement: describe ionic bonding including the examples of sodium chloride, magnesium oxide and calcium fluoride

title: Definition of metallic bonding
statement: define metallic bonding as the electrostatic attraction between positive metal ions and delocalised electrons

title: Covalent and dative covalent bonding
statement: define covalent bonding as electrostatic attraction between the nuclei of two atoms and a shared pair of electrons (a) describe covalent bonding in molecules including: hydrogen $\ce{H2}$, oxygen $\ce{O2}$, nitrogen $\ce{N2}$, chlorine $\ce{Cl2}$, hydrogen chloride $\ce{HCl}$, carbon dioxide $\ce{CO2}$, ammonia $\ce{NH3}$, methane $\ce{CH4}$, ethane $\ce{C2H6}$, ethene $\ce{C2H4}$ (b) understand that elements in period 3 can expand their octet including in the compounds sulfur dioxide $\ce{SO2}$, phosphorus pentachloride $\ce{PCl5}$, and sulfur hexafluoride $\ce{SF6}$ (c) describe coordinate (dative covalent) bonding, including in the reaction between ammonia and hydrogen chloride gases to form the ammonium ion, $\ce{NH4+}$, and in the $\ce{Al2Cl6}$ molecule

title: Sigma and pi bonds, hybridisation
statement: (a) describe covalent bonds in terms of orbital overlap giving $\sigma$ and $\pi$ bonds: $\sigma$ bonds are formed by direct overlap of orbitals between the bonding atoms; $\pi$ bonds are formed by the sideways overlap of adjacent p orbitals above and below the $\sigma$ bond (b) describe how the $\sigma$ and $\pi$ bonds form in molecules including $\ce{H2}$, $\ce{C2H6}$, $\ce{C2H4}$, $\ce{HCN}$ and $\ce{N2}$ (c) use the concept of hybridisation to describe sp, $sp^2$ and $sp^3$ orbitals

title: Bond energy and bond length
statement: (a) define the terms: bond energy as the energy required to break one mole of a particular covalent bond in the gaseous state; bond length as the internuclear distance of two covalently bonded atoms (b) use bond energy values and the concept of bond length to compare the reactivity of covalent molecules

title: VSEPR shapes and bond angles
statement: state and explain the shapes of, and bond angles in, molecules by using VSEPR theory, including as simple examples: $\ce{BF3}$ (trigonal planar, $120°$), $\ce{CO2}$ (linear, $180°$), $\ce{CH4}$ (tetrahedral, $109.5°$), $\ce{NH3}$ (pyramidal, $107°$), $\ce{H2O}$ (non-linear, $104.5°$), $\ce{SF6}$ (octahedral, $90°$), $\ce{PF5}$ (trigonal bipyramidal, $120°$ and $90°$)

title: Predicting shapes of analogous molecules
statement: predict the shapes of, and bond angles in, molecules and ions analogous to those specified in 3.5.1

title: Hydrogen bonding and anomalous water properties
statement: (a) describe hydrogen bonding, limited to molecules containing N-H and O-H groups, including ammonia and water as simple examples (b) use the concept of hydrogen bonding to explain the anomalous properties of $\ce{H2O}$ (ice and water): its relatively high melting and boiling points; its relatively high surface tension; the density of the solid ice compared with the liquid water

title: Electronegativity, bond polarity and dipole moments
statement: use the concept of electronegativity to explain bond polarity and dipole moments of molecules

title: Van der Waals' forces: id-id and pd-pd
statement: (a) describe van der Waals' forces as the intermolecular forces between molecular entities other than those due to bond formation, and use the term van der Waals' forces as a generic term to describe all intermolecular forces (b) describe the types of van der Waals' forces: instantaneous dipole-induced dipole (id-id) forces, also called London dispersion forces; permanent dipole-permanent dipole (pd-pd) forces, including hydrogen bonding (c) describe hydrogen bonding and understand that hydrogen bonding is a special case of permanent dipole-permanent dipole forces between molecules where hydrogen is bonded to a highly electronegative atom

title: Relative strength of bonding versus intermolecular forces
statement: state that, in general, ionic, covalent and metallic bonding are stronger than intermolecular forces

title: Dot-and-cross diagrams
statement: use dot-and-cross diagrams to illustrate ionic, covalent and coordinate bonding including the representation of any compounds stated in 3.4 and 3.5 (dot-and-cross diagrams may include species with atoms which have an expanded octet or species with an odd number of electrons)

title: Origin of gas pressure
statement: explain the origin of pressure in a gas in terms of collisions between gas molecules and the wall of the container

title: Properties of an ideal gas
statement: understand that ideal gases have zero particle volume and no intermolecular forces of attraction

title: Ideal gas equation pV = nRT
statement: state and use the ideal gas equation $pV = nRT$ in calculations, including in the determination of $M_r$

title: Lattice structures of crystalline solids
statement: describe, in simple terms, the lattice structure of a crystalline solid which is: (a) giant ionic, including sodium chloride and magnesium oxide (b) simple molecular, including iodine, buckminsterfullerene $\ce{C60}$ and ice (c) giant molecular, including silicon(IV) oxide, graphite and diamond (d) giant metallic, including copper

title: Structure, bonding and physical properties
statement: describe, interpret and predict the effect of different types of structure and bonding on the physical properties of substances, including melting point, boiling point, electrical conductivity and solubility

title: Deducing structure and bonding from data
statement: deduce the type of structure and bonding present in a substance from given information

title: Exothermic and endothermic reactions
statement: understand that chemical reactions are accompanied by enthalpy changes and these changes can be exothermic ($\Delta H$ is negative) or endothermic ($\Delta H$ is positive)

title: Reaction pathway diagrams
statement: construct and interpret a reaction pathway diagram, in terms of the enthalpy change of the reaction and of the activation energy

title: Standard conditions and enthalpy change terms
statement: define and use the terms: (a) standard conditions (this syllabus assumes that these are $298\text{ K}$ and $101\text{ kPa}$) shown by $\ominus$ (b) enthalpy change with particular reference to: reaction, $\Delta H_r$, formation, $\Delta H_f$, combustion, $\Delta H_c$, neutralisation, $\Delta H_{neut}$

title: Energy transfer from bond breaking and making
statement: understand that energy transfers occur during chemical reactions because of the breaking and making of chemical bonds

title: Calculating enthalpy change from bond energies
statement: use bond energies ($\Delta H$ positive, i.e. bond breaking) to calculate enthalpy change of reaction, $\Delta H_r$

title: Exact versus average bond energies
statement: understand that some bond energies are exact and some bond energies are averages

title: Calculating enthalpy change from experimental data
statement: calculate enthalpy changes from appropriate experimental results, including the use of the relationships $q = mc\Delta T$ and $\Delta H = \dfrac{-mc\Delta T}{n}$

title: Applying Hess's law
statement: apply Hess's law to construct simple energy cycles

title: Calculations using Hess's law cycles
statement: carry out calculations using cycles and relevant energy terms, including: (a) determining enthalpy changes that cannot be found by direct experiment (b) use of bond energy data

title: Calculating oxidation numbers
statement: calculate oxidation numbers of elements in compounds and ions

title: Balancing equations using oxidation numbers
statement: use changes in oxidation numbers to help balance chemical equations

title: Redox, oxidation, reduction and disproportionation
statement: explain and use the terms redox, oxidation, reduction and disproportionation in terms of electron transfer and changes in oxidation number

title: Oxidising and reducing agents
statement: explain and use the terms oxidising agent and reducing agent

title: Roman numeral oxidation number notation
statement: use a Roman numeral to indicate the magnitude of the oxidation number of an element

title: Reversible reactions and dynamic equilibrium
statement: (a) understand what is meant by a reversible reaction (b) understand what is meant by dynamic equilibrium in terms of the rate of forward and reverse reactions being equal and the concentration of reactants and products remaining constant (c) understand the need for a closed system in order to establish dynamic equilibrium

title: Le Chatelier's principle
statement: define Le Chatelier's principle as: if a change is made to a system at dynamic equilibrium, the position of equilibrium moves to minimise this change

title: Applying Le Chatelier's principle
statement: use Le Chatelier's principle to deduce qualitatively (from appropriate information) the effects of changes in temperature, concentration, pressure or presence of a catalyst on a system at equilibrium

title: Equilibrium constant Kc expressions
statement: deduce expressions for equilibrium constants in terms of concentrations, $K_c$

title: Mole fraction and partial pressure
statement: use the terms mole fraction and partial pressure

title: Equilibrium constant Kp expressions
statement: deduce expressions for equilibrium constants in terms of partial pressures, $K_p$ (use of the relationship between $K_p$ and $K_c$ is not required)

title: Calculations using Kc and Kp
statement: use the $K_c$ and $K_p$ expressions to carry out calculations (such calculations will not require the solving of quadratic equations)

title: Calculating equilibrium quantities
statement: calculate the quantities present at equilibrium, given appropriate data

title: Effect of conditions on the equilibrium constant
statement: state whether changes in temperature, concentration or pressure or the presence of a catalyst affect the value of the equilibrium constant for a reaction

title: Haber process and Contact process conditions
statement: describe and explain the conditions used in the Haber process and the Contact process, as examples of the importance of an understanding of dynamic equilibrium in the chemical industry and the application of Le Chatelier's principle

title: Common acids: names and formulas
statement: state the names and formulas of the common acids, limited to hydrochloric acid, $\ce{HCl}$, sulfuric acid, $\ce{H2SO4}$, nitric acid, $\ce{HNO3}$, ethanoic acid, $\ce{CH3COOH}$

title: Common alkalis: names and formulas
statement: state the names and formulas of the common alkalis, limited to sodium hydroxide, $\ce{NaOH}$, potassium hydroxide, $\ce{KOH}$, ammonia, $\ce{NH3}$

title: Brønsted-Lowry theory of acids and bases
statement: describe the Brønsted-Lowry theory of acids and bases

title: Strong versus weak acids and bases
statement: describe strong acids and strong bases as fully dissociated in aqueous solution and weak acids and weak bases as partially dissociated in aqueous solution

title: The pH scale
statement: appreciate that water has pH of 7, acid solutions pH of below 7 and alkaline solutions pH of above 7

title: Behavioural differences between strong and weak acids
statement: explain qualitatively the differences in behaviour between strong and weak acids including the reaction with a reactive metal and difference in pH values by use of a pH meter, universal indicator or conductivity

title: Neutralisation as H+ and OH- forming water
statement: understand that neutralisation reactions occur when $\ce{H+ (aq)}$ and $\ce{OH- (aq)}$ form $\ce{H2O (l)}$

title: Salt formation in neutralisation
statement: understand that salts are formed in neutralisation reactions

title: Sketching pH titration curves
statement: sketch the pH titration curves of titrations using combinations of strong and weak acids with strong and weak alkalis

title: Selecting titration indicators
statement: select suitable indicators for acid-alkali titrations, given appropriate data (pKa values will not be used)

title: Rate of reaction and effective collisions
statement: explain and use the term rate of reaction, frequency of collisions, effective collisions and non-effective collisions

title: Effect of concentration and pressure on rate
statement: explain qualitatively, in terms of frequency of effective collisions, the effect of concentration and pressure changes on the rate of a reaction

title: Calculating rate from experimental data
statement: use experimental data to calculate the rate of a reaction

title: Definition of activation energy
statement: define activation energy, $E_A$, as the minimum energy required for a collision to be effective

title: The Boltzmann distribution
statement: sketch and use the Boltzmann distribution to explain the significance of activation energy

title: Effect of temperature on reaction rate
statement: explain qualitatively, in terms both of the Boltzmann distribution and of frequency of effective collisions, the effect of temperature change on the rate of a reaction

title: Catalysis and activation energy
statement: explain and use the terms catalyst and catalysis: (a) explain that, in the presence of a catalyst, a reaction has a different mechanism, i.e. one of lower activation energy (b) explain this catalytic effect in terms of the Boltzmann distribution (c) construct and interpret a reaction pathway diagram, for a reaction in the presence and absence of an effective catalyst

title: Periodicity of physical properties across Period 3
statement: describe qualitatively (and indicate the periodicity in) the variations in atomic radius, ionic radius, melting point and electrical conductivity of the elements

title: Explaining melting point and conductivity trends
statement: explain the variation in melting point and electrical conductivity in terms of the structure and bonding of the elements

title: Period 3 reactions with oxygen, chlorine and water
statement: describe, and write equations for, the reactions of the elements with oxygen (to give $\ce{Na2O}$, $\ce{MgO}$, $\ce{Al2O3}$, $\ce{P4O10}$, $\ce{SO2}$), chlorine (to give $\ce{NaCl}$, $\ce{MgCl2}$, $\ce{AlCl3}$, $\ce{SiCl4}$, $\ce{PCl5}$) and water (Na and Mg only)

title: Oxidation number trend in Period 3 compounds
statement: state and explain the variation in the oxidation number of the oxides ($\ce{Na2O}$, $\ce{MgO}$, $\ce{Al2O3}$, $\ce{P4O10}$, $\ce{SO2}$ and $\ce{SO3}$ only) and chlorides ($\ce{NaCl}$, $\ce{MgCl2}$, $\ce{AlCl3}$, $\ce{SiCl4}$, $\ce{PCl5}$ only) in terms of their outer shell (valence shell) electrons

title: Reactions of Period 3 oxides with water
statement: describe, and write equations for, the reactions, if any, of the oxides $\ce{Na2O}$, $\ce{MgO}$, $\ce{Al2O3}$, $\ce{SiO2}$, $\ce{P4O10}$, $\ce{SO2}$ and $\ce{SO3}$ with water including the likely pHs of the solutions obtained

title: Acid-base behaviour of Period 3 oxides and hydroxides
statement: describe, explain, and write equations for, the acid/base behaviour of the oxides $\ce{Na2O}$, $\ce{MgO}$, $\ce{Al2O3}$, $\ce{P4O10}$, $\ce{SO2}$ and $\ce{SO3}$ and the hydroxides $\ce{NaOH}$, $\ce{Mg(OH)2}$ and $\ce{Al(OH)3}$ including, where relevant, amphoteric behaviour in reactions with acids and bases (sodium hydroxide only)

title: Reactions of Period 3 chlorides with water
statement: describe, explain, and write equations for, the reactions of the chlorides $\ce{NaCl}$, $\ce{MgCl2}$, $\ce{AlCl3}$, $\ce{SiCl4}$, $\ce{PCl5}$ with water including the likely pHs of the solutions obtained

title: Explaining Period 3 oxide and chloride trends
statement: explain the variations and trends in 9.2.2, 9.2.3, 9.2.4 and 9.2.5 in terms of bonding and electronegativity

title: Deducing bonding type from oxide and chloride properties
statement: suggest the types of chemical bonding present in the chlorides and oxides from observations of their chemical and physical properties

title: Predicting properties from chemical periodicity
statement: predict the characteristic properties of an element in a given group by using knowledge of chemical periodicity

title: Deducing an unknown element from its properties
statement: deduce the nature, possible position in the Periodic Table and identity of unknown elements from given information about physical and chemical properties

title: Group 2 reactions with oxygen, water and acids
statement: describe, and write equations for, the reactions of the elements with oxygen, water and dilute hydrochloric and sulfuric acids

title: Group 2 compounds reacting with water and acids
statement: describe, and write equations for, the reactions of the oxides, hydroxides and carbonates with water and dilute hydrochloric and sulfuric acids

title: Thermal decomposition of Group 2 nitrates and carbonates
statement: describe, and write equations for, the thermal decomposition of the nitrates and carbonates, to include the trend in thermal stabilities

title: Trends in Group 2 element and compound reactions
statement: describe, and make predictions from, the trends in physical and chemical properties of the elements involved in the reactions in 10.1.1 and the compounds involved in 10.1.2, 10.1.3 and 10.1.5

title: Solubility trends of Group 2 hydroxides and sulfates
statement: state the variation in the solubilities of the hydroxides and sulfates

title: Colours and volatility of Group 17 elements
statement: describe the colours and the trend in volatility of chlorine, bromine and iodine

title: Bond strength trend in halogen molecules
statement: describe and explain the trend in the bond strength of the halogen molecules

title: Halogen volatility and induced dipole forces
statement: interpret the volatility of the elements in terms of instantaneous dipole-induced dipole forces

title: Relative reactivity of halogens as oxidising agents
statement: describe the relative reactivity of the elements as oxidising agents

title: Reactions of halogens with hydrogen
statement: describe the reactions of the elements with hydrogen and explain their relative reactivity in these reactions

title: Thermal stability of hydrogen halides
statement: describe the relative thermal stabilities of the hydrogen halides and explain these in terms of bond strengths

title: Relative reactivity of halide ions as reducing agents
statement: describe the relative reactivity of halide ions as reducing agents

title: Testing halide ions with silver and sulfuric acid
statement: describe and explain the reactions of halide ions with: (a) aqueous silver ions followed by aqueous ammonia (the formation and formula of the $\ce{[Ag(NH3)2]+}$ complex is not required) (b) concentrated sulfuric acid, to include balanced chemical equations

title: Chlorine with sodium hydroxide: disproportionation
statement: describe and interpret, in terms of changes in oxidation number, the reaction of chlorine with cold and with hot aqueous sodium hydroxide and recognise these as disproportionation reactions

title: Chlorine in water purification
statement: explain, including by use of an equation, the use of chlorine in water purification to include the production of the active species $\ce{HOCl}$ and $\ce{ClO-}$ which kill bacteria

title: Lack of reactivity of nitrogen
statement: explain the lack of reactivity of nitrogen, with reference to triple bond strength and lack of polarity

title: Basicity of ammonia and the ammonium ion
statement: describe and explain: (a) the basicity of ammonia, using the Brønsted-Lowry theory (b) the structure of the ammonium ion and its formation by an acid-base reaction (c) the displacement of ammonia from ammonium salts by an acid-base reaction

title: Occurrence and catalytic removal of nitrogen oxides
statement: state and explain the natural and man-made occurrences of oxides of nitrogen and their catalytic removal from the exhaust gases of internal combustion engines

title: Nitrogen oxides and photochemical smog
statement: understand that atmospheric oxides of nitrogen ($\ce{NO}$ and $\ce{NO2}$) can react with unburned hydrocarbons to form peroxyacetyl nitrate, PAN, which is a component of photochemical smog

title: Role of nitrogen oxides in acid rain
statement: describe the role of NO and $\ce{NO2}$ in the formation of acid rain both directly and in their catalytic role in the oxidation of atmospheric sulfur dioxide
